title: Vidhura's truth
hookLine: a dice game, a lost bet, and a minister who won't lie his way free
tomorrow: how many little untruths slip out in one ordinary day?

cards: Dice rattle in a cupped hand, then clack across a board. It's the sound of a game night, and in the Jataka it's the sound of a disaster. King Dhananjaya loves to gamble.
A stranger arrives, a yakkha named Punnaka, with a magic jewel and a challenge. The king plays, and loses. Punnaka names his prize: your wise minister, Vidhura.

teach.b: The king panics and looks for a way out. Vidhura isn't mine to give, he says. Ask him.
So they ask Vidhura, in front of the court. Everyone can see the easy answer: say you're your own man.

teach.h: ONE LIE, AND HE WALKS FREE.
teach.b: One sentence, and he walks away safe.

teach.h: HE TELLS THE TRUTH, AND GOES.
teach.b: Vidhura thinks it through and tells the truth as it stands: he serves the king, so he is the king's to wager. And he goes off with Punnaka, out of the city, into real danger. Why would anyone do that?
In the story, his whole life rests on being someone whose word can be trusted, by the king, the court, anyone who asks. One lie to save himself, and every word he'd ever given would be worth less.
The tale doesn't end in his death. In the end his wisdom and calm win over even Punnaka, and he comes home. But he didn't know that when he answered.
That's what true under pressure is: you answer before you know how it ends.
Hear the dice again. Luck runs the game. Vidhura doesn't let luck run his mouth.

how: The Vidhura Jataka is one of the last ten Jataka tales, tied by tradition to the perfection of truthfulness; it is retold in Theravada sermons and is a favorite subject of temple murals.

o: telling the truth when it costs you
a minister's trick to win at dice
a promise kept only when it's easy

games.q: who's who at the dice game — tap the pairs.
p: the yakkha who won the bet
the minister who told the truth

s: Vidhura lied to save himself, then made up for it later
he told the truth in front of the court, though a lie would have set him free.
the king tried to get out of the bet by saying Vidhura wasn't his to give
and Vidhura's own answer settled it.
Vidhura knew the story would end well when he answered
he answered before the ending; that's what makes it truth under pressure.

games.q: in a meeting, your boss asks whether the report was late because of you. it was. a vague answer would pass. what's Vidhura's move?
o: say plainly it was you, and what you'll do about it.
say the deadline was unclear, which is partly true.
stay quiet and let the silence answer for you.
games.why: Vidhura gave the true answer in front of the court, though a lie would have set him free, and before he knew how it would end.

practice: Hold something with some weight in your palm: a coin, a key, a stone. Think of one promise you've made that's due soon, and as you feel the weight, say it to yourself plainly: I said I would, and I will.
Then just hold it, steady, while the sit goes on.

wordCard.voice: Vidhura's truth: telling the truth when it costs you, before you know how the story ends.

orig.note: Pali name of the wise minister of Jataka 545, tied by tradition to truthfulness.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: true under pressure, since the dice decide the game but never the answer. Good night.

sources.ref: Jataka 545, Vidhurapandita Jataka (the dice game with Punnaka; the king's evasion; Vidhura's truthful answer; his return)
